claims.text: An MTP-assisted perturbation free-energy scheme can replace full TOR-TILD for Ta-based refractory BCC high-entropy alloys.
The proposed replacement will achieve more than a fourfold computational speedup.
The proposed scheme will maintain an error below 1 meV/atom for Ta-based refractory BCC HEAs.
Achieving the stated efficiency and accuracy requires training configurations that represent disordered liquids and the relevant multicomponent local chemical environments.
TaVCrW and TaNbHfZr are examples of the targeted Ta-based refractory BCC HEA system.
The targeted alloys are solid at ambient conditions and transition to a liquid near their melting points.
MTPs can be used to aid high-temperature thermodynamic calculations in TaVCrW.
The relevant solid-liquid temperature range extends to approximately 3000 K for the targeted refractory HEAs.
The targeted multicomponent systems exhibit severe lattice distortion.
An MTP trained on liquid configurations captures many-body interactions and local chemical disorder in the liquid phase.
Using an MTP for perturbation steps avoids expensive DFT sampling across the full phase space.
Ensemble averaging over small reference-to-target energy deviations bypasses the slow convergence of full thermodynamic integration.
Success depends on the MTP generalizing to liquid structures outside its training set.
The proposed method will predict the melting free energy within 1 meV/atom of DFT benchmarks.
Liquid radial distribution functions from the proposed method will agree with ab initio molecular dynamics within 5%.
Standard TOR-TILD requires extensive full-phase-space sampling and is computationally prohibitive for multicomponent HEAs.
Training primarily on solid configurations or binary subsystems can produce artifacts in predicted multicomponent liquid structure.
Extreme local liquid compositions can cause MTP extrapolation errors.
The perturbation calculation is accurate only when perturbations remain within a linear-response regime.
Errors above 1 meV/atom or RDF deviations above 10% in the held-out-composition stress test would falsify the hypothesis and indicate a training-set artifact.
